strengths: Elegant theoretical framework: Theorem 4.4 reveals the PLD of random allocation as log of sum of exp-PLDs, enabling efficient computation. Formalization of PLD realization with domination-preserving operations is mathematically rigorous.

Significant practical improvements: Bounds are 10-30% tighter than prior analytical work (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025, Dong et al. 2025) and match Monte Carlo estimates, with demonstrated O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²) complexity.
Generality and extensibility: Algorithms work for arbitrary DP mechanisms, not just Gaussian; PLD realization framework extends naturally to composition and subsampling (Theorems 3.3, 4.4).

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple scenarios (PREAMBLE, privacy-utility tradeoffs, varying parameters), comparisons with both analytical and Monte Carlo bounds, and extensive ablations strengthen confidence.
Complete technical exposition: Full proofs in appendices, detailed algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 1-9), and implementation details support reproducibility and understanding.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: The dominating pair structure (P̄_t) and reduction framework are from prior work (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025, Chua et al. 2024a). The contribution is primarily an algorithmic optimization (log-sum-exp) rather than new theoretical insight.

Incomplete complexity analysis: O(log³(t)) derivation in Theorem 4.6 is not clearly justified; direct analysis suggests O(log⁴(t)). The IQR_β/t factor creates severe scaling challenges for small β that are under-acknowledged.

Limited utility-privacy empirical validation: Paper motivates DP-SGD applications but only repeats toy mean-estimation experiments. No real neural network training validation despite ICML's expectations for ML applications.

Practical algorithmic limitations: (1) Cannot efficiently leverage FFT due to large dynamic range in exp-PLD space (Figure 8 shows FFT sometimes outperforms). (2) Numerical stability requires float128 for δ ≤ 10⁻¹⁵/t. (3) Stochastic domination not preserved under dual/subsampling transformations (Claim B.2), weakening guarantees.

Experimental scope gaps: Evaluation focuses on Gaussian mechanism (generality not empirically validated). PREAMBLE results lack decomposition of improvement sources. No comparison with exact analytical results for special cases. Monte Carlo validation limited to unspecified 'statistically stable' regimes.

Reproducibility concerns: Code availability stated as '(Shenfeld, 2026)'—a forward reference, violating submission-time reproducibility. Numerical stability handling (Kahan summation, float128 heuristics) lacks formal justification and is error-prone.

Presentation and clarity issues: Heavy notation (multiple decorations) makes the paper dense. Practical conditions for random allocation being 'better suited' for DP-SGD are not clearly specified. Figure 7 shows Poisson and allocation don't dominate each other, complicating claimed advantages.

strengths: Addresses a real problem: random allocation has utility advantages over Poisson but prior privacy analyses were loose. This work provides tight, practical bounds.

Novel technical framework: PLD realization (Definition 3.1) is an elegant primitive for numerical accounting. The insight that random allocation PLD = ln of normalized exp-PLD sum (Theorem 4.4) is clever and non-obvious.
Comprehensive theoretical development: Carefully formalizes relationships between stochastic and hockey-stick domination, composition properties, and approximation guarantees (Theorem 4.6).
Significant empirical improvements: Bounds substantially tighter than prior analytical work (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025, Dong et al. 2025), closely matching Monte Carlo estimates in Figure 2.

General applicability: Enables PLD accounting for arbitrary noise distributions and subsampling (Theorem 3.3) without closed-form expressions. PREAMBLE application shows utility for nested algorithms.
Complete implementation: Detailed algorithms (1-9) with pseudocode and numerical stability considerations enable reproducibility.
weaknesses: Critical presentation issues: Dense exposition lacks intuition. Main theorems (4.4, 4.6) presented with heavy notation without explaining why exp-PLDs arise or how the algorithm works conceptually. Multiple domination notions (hockey-stick vs. stochastic) introduced without clear motivation.

Limited practical significance: Random allocation improves ε by ~20% over Poisson (Figure 4 shows nearly overlapping curves), not the substantial advantage hoped for. Incremental advance—dominating pair from Feldman & Shenfeld (2025); contribution is mainly algorithmic.

Computational complexity concerns: O(α⁻²) accuracy scaling is problematic. Paper acknowledges FFT doesn't work well due to multiplicative discretization requirement but doesn't analyze if this limitation is fundamental. Runtime becomes expensive for tight bounds (Figure 3).

Stochastic domination fragility: Claim B.2 shows stochastic domination NOT preserved under dual and subsampling operations (even for PLD realizations), yet framework relies on approximate versions. Implications for overall tightness unclear and inadequately discussed in main text.

Unmotivated technical choices: Why PLD realization requires E[e^{-L}] ≤ 1 and f_L(-∞) = 0 not explained. Discretization strategy (α' and β' parameters) appears ad-hoc rather than principled. Lemma 2.8's lossy reduction from k-out-of-t not quantified.

Incomplete experimental validation: Evaluation focuses exclusively on Gaussian mechanism—extension to discrete mechanisms (Laplace, exponential) unclear. No real ML experiments beyond toy mean-estimation problem. PREAMBLE provides only single application. Monte Carlo baselines used as ground truth without uncertainty quantification.

Excessive appendix relegation: Critical proofs (Claim B.2 on why domination fails under operations) relegated to appendices without main-text implications. This makes it hard to understand when the framework applies.

Missing practical guidance: Figure 7 shows privacy bounds are incomparable in some regimes. Paper doesn't clarify when practitioners should prefer random allocation vs. Poisson, limiting actionable insights.

strengths: Novel and efficient algorithm for computing PLD of random allocation using exp-PLD convolutions; O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²) complexity is practically achievable compared to infeasible Monte Carlo or loose analytical bounds
Tight empirical bounds that closely match lower bounds and Monte Carlo estimates, consistently improving on prior analytical methods (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025, Dong et al. 2025)
General PLD realization framework (Definition 3.1) extends privacy accounting beyond composition to subsampling and random allocation with formal domination-preserving operations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple parameter regimes with comparisons to multiple baselines, including practical application to PREAMBLE algorithm
Full implementation details in appendix with code availability, enabling reproducibility and practical adoption
Mathematically rigorous treatment with careful analysis of stochastic domination, approximation parameters (α,β), and tightness preservation through transformations
weaknesses: Contribution is primarily computational rather than theoretical: privacy amplification of random allocation was already established in prior work; this provides efficient computation but not new privacy insights
Modest practical improvements: privacy gains over Poisson sampling are typically <5-10% in most regimes (Figures 1-2), raising questions about whether computational cost justifies the improvements

Inherent approximation in method: computes (α,β)-tight upper bounds rather than exact values; trade-off between discretization parameters and computation time deserves deeper analysis and practical guidance for parameter selection
Lower bounds analyzed only briefly (Remark 4.7); formal proof of optimality would strengthen claims about tightness; lower bound algorithm not given the same rigor as upper bounds
Numerical stability issues for δ ≤ 10^{-15}/t requiring float128; practical frequency and impact of this limitation not quantified, suggesting method may have robustness limitations
Section 3 on PLD realizations is quite abstract; distinction between hockey-stick domination and stochastic domination needs clearer early exposition to aid readership
Algorithm design choices (e.g., α' = α/(2⌈log₂(t)⌉+1) in Algorithm 6) lack justification; limited guidance on how practitioners should select discretization parameters
